questions.text: In a running bond pattern for multi-wythe walls, what is the primary structural function of header courses?

options.text: To increase the horizontal tensile strength of individual courses
To tie parallel wythes together to ensure composite action
To reduce the quantity of mortar required
To simplify construction by eliminating bed joints

rationale.a: Tension in masonry is primarily handled by reinforcement, not the orientation of units.
rationale.c: Header courses do not significantly reduce mortar consumption.
rationale.d: Bed joints are always required in standard masonry regardless of the unit orientation.
rationale.correct: Headers are units laid perpendicular to the wall plane. Their primary job is to provide a mechanical tie between parallel wythes so the wall resists loads as a single structural unit. [cite: 7, 20]

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015 Section 707.2; PD 1096 Rule VIII Section 804

questions.text: Compare English bond and Flemish bond in terms of their mechanical bonding capacity for multi-wythe walls.

options.text: English bond provides more frequent header-ties (alternating header/stretcher courses) than Flemish bond.
Flemish bond is structurally superior to English bond because it uses more mortar, which is believed to enhance the wall's overall stability
Both are inferior to stack bond in Seismic Zone 4, where lateral forces are a significant concern for structural integrity
Running bond is the only pattern allowed in the Philippines, according to local building regulations

rationale.b: Mortar quantity does not dictate structural superiority; the arrangement of units (bond) does.
rationale.c: Stack bond is the weakest of all patterns and is restricted in Zone 4.
rationale.d: While Running Bond is the most common, English and Flemish bonds are legally permissible and structurally sound.
rationale.correct: English bond consists of alternating courses of all-headers and all-stretchers, resulting in a high density of transverse ties. Flemish bond alternates headers and stretchers within the same course, providing strong but less frequent bonding than the English bond. [cite: 7, 13]
rationale.takeaway: English Bond = maximum transverse header frequency.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015 Section 702; PD 1096 Rule VIII Section 804

questions.text: A continuous vertical section of masonry one unit thick is called a ___. In a cavity wall, there are typically two of these parallel sections separated by an air space.

options.text: Cell
Wythe
Course
Header

rationale.a: Cells are the voids within a Concrete Hollow Block (CHB).
rationale.c: A course is a continuous horizontal layer of masonry units.
rationale.d: A header is a masonry unit laid with its longest dimension perpendicular to the wall face.
rationale.correct: A wythe is a continuous vertical section of masonry one unit in thickness. Cavity walls consist of two wythes (inner and outer) separated by a cavity. [cite: 7, 15]
rationale.takeaway: Wythe = vertical section; Course = horizontal layer.

questions.text: In concrete hollow block (CHB) masonry, which of the following best describes a cell?

options.text: The horizontal mortar joint between courses, which provides stability and alignment for the masonry units
The air space between two wythes, often used for insulation or to accommodate reinforcement bars
The enclosed void within an individual masonry unit
The bond pattern connecting units, which can vary to enhance structural integrity and aesthetic appeal

rationale.b: This is a cavity or collar joint.
rationale.d: Bond patterns refer to the arrangement of units (e.g., Running, Stack).
rationale.correct: Cells (or cores) are the hollow voids in CHBs. Per NSCP 2015, these are often reinforced with vertical bars and filled with grout to enhance structural capacity. [cite: 23, 44]
rationale.takeaway: Cell = core/void in a hollow unit.

questions.text: A masonry inspector in the Philippines finds a two-wythe wall relying solely on mortar in the collar joint for bonding, with no header units or metal ties. Does this comply with Philippine codes?

options.text: Yes, if the mortar is high-strength Type M or S, which can provide sufficient bonding strength in certain conditions
No, both PD 1096 and NSCP 2015 require mechanical bonding via headers or ties for multi-wythe walls.
Yes, if the wall is a non-bearing partition, as structural requirements are less stringent
Yes, but only in Seismic Zone 2, where seismic forces are considered moderate and less demanding

rationale.a: Mortar grade increases local compressive strength but does not provide the perpendicular 'tie' required for composite action.
rationale.c: Even non-bearing walls must resist out-of-plane wind and seismic forces; bonding is still required.
rationale.d: High seismic risk in the Philippines (Zone 4) makes these mechanical ties absolutely mandatory for safety.
rationale.correct: Per NSCP 2015 Section 707.2.2 and PD 1096 Rule VIII Section 804, multi-wythe walls must be bonded with masonry headers or non-corrosive metal ties. Mortar adhesion alone is insufficient for structural bonding in multi-story or seismic applications. [cite: 44]
rationale.takeaway: Mortar alone is not a structural tie between wythes.

questions.text: Which bond pattern requires specific continuous horizontal reinforcement in Seismic Zone 4 (high seismic risk) because of its lack of natural interlock?

options.text: English bond
Flemish bond
Stack bond
Running bond

rationale.a: English bond provides strong mechanical interlock through alternating header/stretcher courses.
rationale.b: Flemish bond provides interlock through alternating units in each course.
rationale.d: Running bond is the standard interlocking pattern where head joints are offset by at least 1/4 of the unit length.
rationale.correct: Stack bond has vertical head joints that align. In high seismic zones (Seismic Zone 4), the NSCP 2015 requires stack bond walls to have continuous horizontal reinforcement to compensate for the lack of overlapping units. [cite: 42, 44]
rationale.takeaway: Stack bond lacks overlap and requires extra reinforcement in high seismic zones.

questions.text: According to the NSCP 2015, the air space (cavity) in a cavity wall must comply with which of the following dimension limits?

options.text: Minimum 25 mm to maximum 75 mm
Minimum 50 mm to maximum 115 mm
Minimum 100 mm to maximum 200 mm
Any dimension provided it is filled with grout

rationale.a: 25 mm is too narrow for proper moisture drainage and tie placement.
rationale.c: 100 mm is near the maximum limit; 200 mm is too wide for standard wall ties to act effectively.
rationale.d: If the cavity is filled with grout, it is no longer defined as a cavity wall but as a 'grouted multi-wythe wall.'
rationale.correct: NSCP 2015 Section 707.1.4.2 explicitly states that the minimum thickness of the cavity shall be 50 mm and the maximum thickness shall be 115 mm. [cite: 44]
rationale.takeaway: NSCP Cavity Limits: 50 mm to 115 mm.

questions.text: A structural engineer specifies that for a building in Seismic Zone 4, cells at header courses must be solid-grouted. What is the structural rationlea for this in a cavity wall?

options.text: Grout in header course cells increases the axial load capacity of headers and provides lateral continuity.
Grout creates vertical load paths and solidifies the lateral tie between wythes.
Grouting increases the compressive strength uniformly across all wythes.
Grouting cells eliminates the need for wall ties.

rationale.a: While it increases axial capacity, the main seismic concern is shear transfer and wythe continuity.
rationale.c: Compressive strength increase is a benefit, but the spacing and placement targets lateral stability.
rationale.d: Grouting header cells complements but does not necessarily eliminate the requirement for metal wall ties unless specifically engineered as a bonded wall.
rationale.correct: In Seismic Zone 4, the integration of grout and reinforcement is critical. Solidly grouting the cells where headers occur ensures that the 'bridge' between the two wythes is stiff and capable of transferring seismic shear forces. [cite: 2, 44]
rationale.takeaway: Grout at headers ensures wythes act together during seismic sway.

questions.text: What is the structural difference between cavity wall construction and single-wythe masonry in terms of lateral load resistance?

options.text: Single-wythe walls act as a monolithic unit; cavity walls require mechanical headers or ties to prevent wythes from acting independently.
Cavity walls have inherently greater strength because of the air space insulation, which provides additional thermal resistance and moisture control.
Headers function identically in both; they are used only for aesthetic texture, and do not contribute to structural integrity or lateral load resistance.
Cavity walls do not require ties if the cavity is filled with moisture-resistant insulation, which is assumed to provide sufficient structural stability.

rationale.b: Air space provides thermal and moisture benefits, but actually complicates structural load transfer.
rationale.c: Headers in single-wythe walls are purely decorative; in multi-wythe walls, they are structural ties.
rationale.d: Insulation has no structural bonding capacity; mechanical ties or headers are always required.
rationale.correct: A single-wythe wall is a solid, continuous mass. A cavity wall consists of two distinct leaves; without headers or ties, each leaf would buckle or sway independently, significantly reducing the total lateral resistance. [cite: 2, 7, 15]
rationale.takeaway: Composite action in cavity walls requires mechanical connection.

questions.text: Which joint type separates two parallel wythes in a cavity wall and may be filled with mortar, grout, or left as air space?

options.text: Bed joint, typically used to provide horizontal alignment and support for masonry units
Collar joint
Head joint, which is primarily vertical and helps in aligning the masonry units vertically
Shear joint, designed to resist lateral forces and provide stability in the structure

rationale.a: Bed joints are the horizontal layers of mortar on which masonry units are laid.
rationale.c: Head joints are the vertical mortar joints between ends of masonry units in the same course.
rationale.d: Shear joint is not a standard masonry definition used for the space between wythes.
rationale.correct: The collar joint is the longitudinal vertical space between wythes of masonry units. Per PD 1096, it may be filled with mortar or grout to create a composite wall or left as an air space in a cavity wall. [cite: 44]
rationale.takeaway: Collar joint = vertical space between wythes.
